PullRequest.Title: mcp: initial data flow for MCP gateway
PullRequest.Body:
Adds base startGateway method and data flows. Currently the route is just a stub.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The proxy argument packaging, both reachable local/remote call paths, scalar-string Map keys, early return on lookup miss, and lifetime fallback are all directly established in repository code. Only the rate of repeated gateway creation varies by extension workload.
Findings.PerformanceResource: McpGatewayRoute objects and ownership entries retained in two Maps, plus the localhost HTTP server/socket and accumulated log/cleanup work
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Retention grows linearly with each startMcpGateway()/dispose() cycle during the lifetime of one renderer or remote connection; disconnect cleanup later scans all historically retained entries.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Retained memory and an HTTP listener that never shuts down after normal disposal, with increasing disconnect-cleanup CPU/log I/O as gateway churn accumulates.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no gateway API, route registry, ownership map, or gateway HTTP listener to retain across extension operations.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: ProxyChannel.toService packages disposeGateway(info.gatewayId) as the argument array [gatewayId], but the new custom channel casts that whole array to string and passes it as the Map key. The lookup always misses, so normal disposal removes nothing and cannot stop the server.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 39 passes `args as string` directly to `disposeGateway`; the newly added proxy call path supplies `[info.gatewayId]`, while the newly added service stores entries under the scalar UUID string.
Findings.Title: Unwrap the IPC arguments before disposing the gateway
Findings.Impact: An extension that creates a gateway for each agent/task and disposes it afterward leaks one route and ownership record per task until the window or remote connection disconnects; even after the final public gateway is disposed, the localhost server remains live.
Findings.Evidence: ProxyChannel.toService invokes channel.call(propKey, methodArgs), where methodArgs is an array. Both desktop-local and remote workbench implementations call the proxied disposeGateway(info.gatewayId), reaching this channel. This changed line passes args (the array) to McpGatewayService.disposeGateway, whose string-keyed _gateways.get(gatewayId) misses and returns before deleting either Map or calling _stopServer(). Disconnect cleanup is only a later connection-lifetime fallback.
Findings.Recommendation: Type `args` as an argument tuple/array and pass its first element (for example, `const [gatewayId] = args as [string]`) to disposeGateway; retain the channel context injection only for createGateway.

Scenarios.Scenario: VS Code startup in desktop or remote-server mode before any extension requests a gateway
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Static gateway modules are loaded and the service/channel is instantiated during process service setup, but the McpGatewayService constructor only initializes Maps; no HTTP bind or cross-process call is required before startup can progress.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One service and one channel per main/remote server process, independent of workspace size or MCP server count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: No gateway work is scheduled; there is no queue or concurrent boundary operation in this scenario.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The shared service starts empty. There is no cold server creation until createGateway is called and no cache lookup on startup.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: service registration and constructors are directly visible, and http.createServer/listen occur only inside the create path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Module parse/instantiation cost is small and unmeasured, but no heavyweight boundary is reachable here.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable startup regression; registration is eager but the network server and route allocation remain demand-driven.

Scenarios.Scenario: An extension calls startMcpGateway on desktop, remote desktop, or browser connected to a remote server
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The extension-host RPC must reach MainThreadMcp, then one local-main or remote-agent channel call must complete; on a cold service the localhost HTTP listen event must also complete before the URI is returned. Warm calls skip listen and allocate only a new route/IDs.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Extension host invokes MainThreadMcp.$startMcpGateway and receives gateway metadata.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly one extension-host RPC per API call; no grouping or deduplication because each call intentionally creates a unique gateway.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The API and RPC did not exist before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Blocking: the API promise cannot resolve until the main-thread result returns.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Workbench calls the main-process or remote-server gateway channel.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One platform channel call per successful API call.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Blocking: gateway metadata is returned only after service creation completes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Binds an HTTP server to a random localhost port and waits for the listening event.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One listen on the first gateway after the service has zero gateways; zero for warm calls while the shared server is listening. Concurrent cold starts share _serverStartPromise.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cold-path blocking; warm gateway creation does not cross this boundary.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of explicit gateway starts. Effective server-bind cardinality is one per nonempty gateway lifetime, while route/ownership cardinality is one per call.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Concurrent cold starts are coalesced by _serverStartPromise. After startup, route allocations are synchronous on the Node event loop; IPC calls can arrive concurrently but do not fan out to additional boundaries.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The shared listening server is the warm state. There is no route deduplication or negative cache because every API call intentionally receives a unique route. A failed start clears _serverStartPromise for retry.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: both local/remote call paths and cold/warm guards are directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Actual localhost bind and remote IPC latency vary by host, but call count and critical-path placement are explicit.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding on creation: the expensive cold bind is shared and concurrent cold starts are coalesced.

Scenarios.Scenario: An extension disposes gateways while its window or remote connection remains alive
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Public dispose sends one extension-host RPC; MainThreadMcp removes its result and invokes one main-process/remote IPC disposal for the first dispose of that gateway. That platform disposal should remove the route and close the HTTP server after the last gateway, but the custom channel passes the proxy's argument array as the scalar Map key, so cleanup never occurs.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Requests disposal in the workbench and deletes the workbench-side disposable result.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One extension-host RPC per public dispose call; the workbench forwards at most one platform disposal for each known gateway ID because its DisposableMap entry is deleted.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No gateway disposal RPC or retained gateway resources existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the critical path because dispose returns void, but it initiates required resource cleanup.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Sends the gateway ID to the local main process or remote server for route disposal.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One downstream call per distinct gateway removed from MainThreadMcp; ProxyChannel encodes it as the one-element array [gatewayId].
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No channel or platform gateway maps existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Fire-and-forget from the disposable; failure does not block the caller and leaves platform resources retained.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Would close the localhost HTTP listener when the final route is removed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Changed behavior performs zero closes on normal explicit disposal because every scalar-key lookup misses; intended behavior is one close after the final live gateway.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the caller's critical path, but determines listener/socket lifetime.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Distinct start/dispose cycles during one long-lived renderer or remote connection. The effective retained cardinality equals the number of successfully started gateways, not the number currently exposed to extensions.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Disposals are not awaited and have no backpressure, but the leak is deterministic even for sequential calls; concurrency is not required.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The workbench DisposableMap evicts its ID, but the platform _gateways and _gatewayToClient Maps never evict on explicit disposal. Disconnect cleanup is the only eventual lifetime fallback and scans/removes all entries owned by that connection.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: ProxyChannel's array encoding, the custom channel cast, string-keyed lookup, early return, and missed server shutdown are directly established.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Extensions may create one long-lived gateway or repeatedly create per task/agent session; that prevalence controls severity, not the proven linear retention mechanism.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable medium unbounded-retention regression; one finding was submitted on the changed channel line.

Scenarios.Scenario: A renderer or remote-agent connection disconnects after creating gateways
Scenarios.CriticalPath: IPCServer.onDidRemoveConnection synchronously scans the ownership Map, gathers entries matching the connection context, removes them, and initiates server close if no global routes remain. This is cleanup triggered after the connection is already lost, not a user workflow critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Closes the localhost HTTP listener after owned routes are removed and no routes remain.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one close per disconnect cleanup; Map scan cardinality is all retained gateway ownership entries across connected clients.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No gateway ownership scan or listener close existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off normal interaction paths, though the synchronous O(G) scan runs on the main/remote server event loop.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Total gateway ownership entries G. Because explicit disposal is broken, G includes historical starts for all still-connected clients rather than only live gateways.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One synchronous scan per connection-removal event; no batching across simultaneous disconnects, and each event independently scans the current Map.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Disconnect cleanup finally evicts matching entries. There is no separate index by client, so cleanup scans the full Map; normal disposal should have kept G bounded but does not.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: event registration and full-Map iteration are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Disconnect frequency and historical gateway count vary, but the O(G) fallback cost is secondary to the reported retention root cause.
Scenarios.Verdict: Covered by the disposal finding rather than reported separately; fixing scalar-ID disposal bounds this cleanup to genuinely live gateways.

Scenarios.Scenario: An external process sends HTTP requests to a created gateway route
Scenarios.CriticalPath: One localhost network request is parsed, followed by an O(1) route Map lookup and the current stub's immediate JSON 501 response. No extension-host IPC, subprocess, filesystem, database, or downstream network operation is reached by the stub.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Receives and responds to one localhost HTTP request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One ingress and one response per external request; no fan-out and no cache-dependent repetition.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The direct response is the complete request critical path.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: External request rate and concurrent connections; each current request performs constant-time routing and a small JSON response.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Node's HTTP server accepts requests without an explicit limiter, but the stub does no blocking or scaling downstream work, so no concrete concurrency burst is established.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Route lookup uses the in-memory Map. There is no response cache; positive and negative requests both perform one lookup and immediate response.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the current stub path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Future route implementation may add expensive work, but it is outside this diff; current request work is bounded.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable request-path regression beyond the already reported leaked route/server lifetime.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 16 changed files and all diff pages. Traced startup, local/remote creation, explicit disposal, disconnect cleanup, and HTTP request paths. Submitted one high-confidence medium finding for deterministic unbounded gateway retention caused by incorrect ProxyChannel argument handling; found no concrete performance regression in cold-start coalescing or the bounded request stub.
